procedural_history.impugned_order: Remand Order dated 04.10.2023 passed by the Ld. Special Judge, Patiala House Court
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 7278 of 2023 in the High Court of Delhi challenging the Remand Order. The learned Single Judge of the High Court of Delhi dismissed the Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 7278 of 2023 vide judgment dated 13th October, 2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, assailing the order dated 13th October, 2023 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Delhi. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The arrest of the appellant followed by remand order dated 4th October, 2023 and so also the impugned order passed by the High Court of Delhi dated 13th October, 2023 are hereby declared to be invalid in the eyes of law and are quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the arrest and subsequent remand of the accused-appellant was vitiated as the copy of the remand application was not provided to him or his counsel before passing of the order of remand thus, not informing him of the grounds of arrest in writing.

facts: The appellant was arrested on October 3, 2023, and presented before a Remand Judge at his residence before 6:00 a.m. the next day.
The remand order was passed at 6:00 a.m. on October 4, 2023.

The copy of the remand application, which contained the written grounds of arrest, was sent to the appellant's chosen advocate via WhatsApp only after the remand order had already been passed (around 7:00 a.m.).
The Court found that the entire exercise was done in a "clandestine manner" to prevent the appellant and his lawyer from effectively opposing the police custody request.
The Court noted that the arrest memo itself did not convey the specific grounds for the arrest.
law: Article 22(1) of the Constitution of India provides a fundamental right to be informed of the grounds of arrest.
The Supreme Court held that the requirement to communicate the grounds of arrest in writing is "sacrosanct and cannot be breached under any situation."
Non-compliance with this constitutional and statutory mandate renders the arrest and subsequent custody illegal.
The Court applied its previous ruling in Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India, which established the necessity of providing written grounds of arrest.
application: The Court analyzed the timeline of events and established as a matter of fact that the remand order was passed at 6:00 a.m., before the appellant or his counsel received the remand application containing the written grounds of arrest.

By not providing the grounds of arrest in writing beforehand, the authorities deprived the appellant of his constitutional right and prevented him and his lawyer from meaningfully opposing the remand and seeking bail.
The Court concluded that any opportunity for a hearing provided after the remand order was already passed was merely an "exercise in futility."
The failure to follow this mandatory procedure was not a mere technicality but a violation of a fundamental right that vitiated the entire process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the failure to provide a copy of the remand application, containing the written grounds of arrest, to the accused-appellant or his counsel before the remand order was passed, was a violation of his fundamental rights. This procedural and constitutional failure vitiated (invalidated) both the arrest and the subsequent remand order, leading the Court to quash them and order the appellant's release.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the arrest and subsequent remand of the accused-appellant was vitiated as the copy of the remand application was not provided to him or his counsel before passing of the order of remand thus, not informing him of the grounds of arrest in writing.
appellant_arguments: The proceedings of arrest and remand were invalid because the appellant was not provided with a copy of the remand application, which contains the grounds of arrest in writing, before the remand order was passed.
respondent_arguments: According to the appellant's own pleadings, he was remanded after 7:00 a.m., so he cannot claim the remand was illegal or that grounds of arrest were not conveyed in writing.

The appellant's advocate sent a written objection against the police custody remand via WhatsApp, which the Remand Judge noted in the order, proving that the remand was opposed and the order is not illegal.
Any illegality or irregularity in the initial arrest and remand is now cured because the investigation is complete and a charge sheet has been filed, meaning the appellant is no longer prejudiced.

There is a presumption of correctness for judicial acts, and the remand order explicitly notes that the appellant's advocate was heard and the grounds of arrest were conveyed; this official record should not be doubted.

cases.principle: The grounds of arrest must be conveyed to the accused in writing, and failure to do so violates the right guaranteed under Article 22 of the Constitution.

cases.principle: To establish the consistent view of the Court that grounds of arrest or detention must be communicated to the person concerned.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The constitutional and statutory requirement to communicate the grounds of arrest or detention in writing to a person is sacrosanct, and non-compliance will render the custody or detention illegal.
obiter: Furnishing a copy of the written grounds of arrest is advisable as a matter of principle to prevent disputes where it may boil down to the word of the arrested person against the arresting officer.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: To give true meaning and purpose to the constitutional and statutory mandate of informing an arrested person of the grounds of arrest under Article 22(1) of the Constitution and Section 19(1) of the Act of 2002, it is necessary that a copy of such written grounds be furnished to the arrested person as a matter of course and without exception. The form of communication where an investigating officer merely reads out or permits the reading of the grounds of arrest is not adequate to fulfill this mandate. Non-compliance with the sacrosanct requirement to provide the grounds of arrest in writing renders the custody and detention illegal.
legal_tests_applied: The requirement to communicate the grounds of arrest or detention in writing to a person, as provided under Articles 22(1) and 22(5) of the Constitution of India, is sacrosanct and cannot be breached under any situation.
Non-compliance with the constitutional requirement and statutory mandate to provide grounds of arrest in writing leads to the custody or detention being rendered illegal.

The interpretation of Article 22(1) of the Constitution and Section 19(1) of the Act of 2002 establishes a mandatory procedural rule: a copy of the written grounds of arrest must be furnished to the arrested person.
policy_considerations: Furnishing a written copy of the grounds of arrest prevents a situation where a dispute over whether the grounds were orally communicated boils down to the word of the arrested person against the word of the authorized officer.

The very purpose of the constitutional and statutory protection to be informed of the grounds of arrest would be rendered nugatory by permitting authorities to merely read out the grounds, irrespective of their length and detail, and claim due compliance.
